passage:
Note from the class teacher, first week.
On his first morning Sachin stood by the window and watched the others, twisting the hem of his shirt. His eyes kept going to Yash, who was lining up shells on the nature table. Twice Sachin took a step towards the table and stopped.
At activity time I paired the children to wash the paint pots. I put Sachin with Yash. They filled the tub together and Yash showed him how to squeeze the brush. By lunch they were sitting side by side. I will keep using pair jobs this week.

qa.q: What was Yash lining up on the nature table?
qa.a: He was lining up shells.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling as he stood by the window?
qa.a: He felt shy but curious about the other children: he twisted his shirt hem, watched Yash and stepped towards the table twice before stopping.

qa.q: Why did the teacher's pair job work well?
qa.a: Washing paint pots together gave Sachin and Yash an easy reason to talk, so a friendship could start without Sachin having to walk up alone.

qa.q: How might Yash see the new boy at the wash tub?
qa.a: Yash probably sees a helper to show things to, since he shows Sachin how to squeeze the brush and later sits with him.

grounding: On his first days a shy, curious child watches the others wondering who will be his friend, and the teacher pairs him with a classmate for a task.

passage:
The village school had one big room and a long mat. Pankaj sat at the very end of it on his first day. He looked at the boys by the door, then at the girls near the blackboard, then at a boy with a torn slate who was humming. Pankaj pulled his knees up and did not say anything.
The teacher poured a heap of seeds onto the mat. "Two by two! Sort the tamarind from the beans. Pankaj, you go with Hrithik."
The humming boy shuffled over. They sorted in silence, then raced. Hrithik let out a laugh. So did Pankaj.

qa.q: What did the teacher ask the pairs to sort?
qa.a: Tamarind seeds from the beans.

qa.q: What does Pankaj pulling his knees up suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt shy and a bit unsure, even while he was curiously looking round at who might be a friend.

qa.q: How could a teacher help other new children like Pankaj?
qa.a: Give them a simple job with a partner, like sorting seeds, so they have something to do together before they have to talk.

qa.q: What might it be like for Hrithik to be paired with the new boy?
qa.a: Hrithik may feel curious about Pankaj too, and the race turns the silence into shared fun.

grounding: A shy, curious child on his first school day wonders who will be his friend, and the teacher pairs him with a classmate for a sorting task.

passage:
"Aadhya, your Nani Sarita was nine once, and silly. My best friend Kamala began walking home with a new girl, Leela. Every time Kamala laughed at Leela's jokes, my stomach knotted like a rope.
So I sulked. I stopped saving Kamala a place at prayer. Worse, I told two girls that Leela copied her sums. It was not true.
Kamala heard. She walked with Leela even more after that, and she would not look at me.
One evening I stood at Kamala's gate and said, 'I miss you. I was jealous.' I told the two girls I had lied. It took weeks, but Kamala came back to the prayer line."

qa.q: What lie did young Sarita tell about Leela?
qa.a: She told two girls that Leela copied her sums.

qa.q: Why did young Sarita stop saving Kamala a place at prayer?
qa.a: She felt jealous and hurt, with her stomach knotting whenever Kamala laughed with Leela, and sulking was how the hurt came out.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Saying "I miss you. I was jealous" at Kamala's gate and owning up to the lie, because honesty brought Kamala back while sulking and rumours had pushed her away.

qa.q: How might Kamala have felt when she heard the lie about Leela?
qa.a: Kamala may have felt angry and protective of Leela, which is why she walked with Leela even more and would not look at Sarita.

grounding: A grandmother recalls feeling jealous when her best friend laughed with a new girl; sulking and a rumour pushed the friend away, and saying she missed her helped.

passage:
The school trip bus was loud and hot, and Gargi's seat was two rows behind Tsering's. Tsering had sat with the new girl, Hema. Every time they laughed, Gargi's stomach twisted.
Rafiq leaned across the aisle. "Let's tell everyone Hema's a copycat. Then Tsering will come back to you."
Gargi's face burned. She wanted to say yes. Instead she shook her head. "No. That's mean."
At the lunch stop, with only ten minutes before the bus left again, Gargi found Tsering by the water tank. Her voice wobbled. "I miss you. Can I sit near you two on the way back?"
Tsering blinked, then smiled. "Of course. Hema likes riddles, you'll see."

qa.q: How long was the lunch stop before the bus left again?
qa.a: Only ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when Rafiq suggested calling Hema a copycat?
qa.a: She felt tempted and ashamed at once: her face burned and she wanted to say yes, but she knew it was mean.

qa.q: Why was Gargi's choice at the water tank wiser than Rafiq's plan?
qa.a: Saying "I miss you" was honest and let Tsering stay close, while a rumour about Hema would likely have pushed Tsering away.

qa.q: How might Tsering see Gargi's question at the water tank?
qa.a: Tsering seems glad and relieved, maybe not having noticed Gargi was hurting, and happily includes her with Hema.

grounding: A girl's stomach twists when her best friend laughs with a new girl; she refuses to spread a rumour and says she misses her friend instead.

passage:
"Varun, sit. Your Himani Masi once nearly lost her best friend by holding on too tight. In Class 5, Chitra started doing homework with a new girl after school. I was terrified she'd forget me. So I watched her. Every morning: 'Who did you sit with? Why?' I even said, 'If you're really my friend, don't talk to her at lunch.'
One day Chitra snapped, 'It's like I'm in a cage with you!' and walked off.
That night I wrote down what I actually felt. Next day I told her, 'I feel left out. Can Sundays be just us?' She hugged me. We still speak every Sunday."

qa.q: What did young Himani ask Chitra every morning?
qa.a: She asked, "Who did you sit with? Why?"

qa.q: What was young Himani afraid of when Chitra made a new friend?
qa.a: She was terrified of being replaced and forgotten, which is why she watched Chitra and tested her loyalty.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped, and why?
qa.a: Telling Chitra plainly "I feel left out" and asking for Sundays just together, because it asked for time without controlling who Chitra could talk to.

qa.q: How did Himani's checking and testing feel to Chitra?
qa.a: Chitra felt trapped, saying it was like being in a cage, and she walked off.

grounding: An aunt recalls fearing her best friend would replace her, clinging and testing her loyalty until the friend felt trapped, then saying plainly she felt left out and asking for one plan together.

passage:
This year Parveen was put in section B, and Joseph stayed in A. They only had the fifteen-minute break together, and on Monday Parveen spent it with Mehak from her new class.
By Thursday Joseph was waiting outside section B before the bell. "Who are you sitting with? Is it Mehak again?" He followed her to the tap and back.
Parveen stopped. "Joseph, you're like a guard. I can't even breathe."
Joseph's face went hot. He walked away and kicked a stone. At home he practised the words.
Friday he said, "I feel left out since you moved. Could we cycle on Saturday, just us?"
Parveen nodded. "Yes. I miss that too."

qa.q: Which section was Parveen put in this year?
qa.a: She was put in section B.

qa.q: What was Joseph afraid of when he waited outside section B?
qa.a: He was afraid Mehak would replace him as Parveen's friend, and that fear made him cling and check on her.

qa.q: What did Joseph change that worked better?
qa.a: He stopped checking and said plainly that he felt left out, then asked for one plan together: cycling on Saturday.

qa.q: How did Joseph's checking feel to Parveen?
qa.a: She felt watched and trapped, telling him he was like a guard and she could not breathe.

grounding: A boy afraid of being replaced clings to his best friend and checks who she sits with; she feels trapped, and he then tells her plainly he feels left out and asks for one plan together.

passage:
Abhinav had spent three lunch breaks helping Noor, the new girl, with the class model of the solar system. It was due Friday, and they were racing to finish. Meanwhile Lakshmi, his friend since nursery, had stopped waiting for him at the gate. When he waved, she looked away.
Abhinav's chest felt tight. Was he supposed to stop helping Noor? He hated feeling pulled in two.
On Thursday, with the glue still drying, he ran to catch Lakshmi. "You're still my best friend. Can we do our Saturday kite flying like always? And maybe Noor can come for a bit?"
Lakshmi kicked the gate post. Then she nodded.

qa.q: What were Abhinav and Noor making?
qa.a: The class model of the solar system.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Abhinav have when Lakshmi looked away?
qa.a: He felt guilty and cornered, as if he had to choose between helping Noor and keeping Lakshmi.

qa.q: What did Abhinav do that was kind to both girls?
qa.a: He reassured Lakshmi she was still his best friend, kept their Saturday kite flying, and invited Noor along instead of dropping her.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have seen Abhinav's three lunch breaks with Noor?
qa.a: Lakshmi may have felt left behind and worried she was being replaced, which is why she stopped waiting at the gate.

grounding: A boy's best friend turns cold after he makes a new friend; he feels guilty and cornered, then reassures her, keeps their special time and invites the new girl in.

passage:
In their Pune housing colony, Nilesh and Ishita had shared the same swing since they were five. Then Farah moved into the next building, and Nilesh started teaching her to skate in the parking lot.
Now Ishita walked past without saying hello. At the water cooler she gave one-word answers. Nilesh felt his stomach drop each time, as if he had done something wrong and didn't know how to fix it.
On Sunday he knocked at Ishita's door with two ice lollies. "I missed you this week. Swing at five, like always? And Farah wants to learn our hand-clap game, if you'll show her."
Ishita took a lolly. "Only if I teach it," she said.

qa.q: What was Nilesh teaching Farah in the parking lot?
qa.a: He was teaching her to skate.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when Ishita walked past without saying hello?
qa.a: He felt guilty and stuck, his stomach dropping as if he had done something wrong and didn't know how to fix it.

qa.q: What small step helped Nilesh, and why?
qa.a: He went to Ishita with ice lollies, said he missed her, kept their swing time, and invited her to teach Farah, so she felt valued instead of replaced.

qa.q: How might Ishita see Farah before and after the Sunday visit?
qa.a: Before, Ishita may see Farah as a threat taking her friend; after, Farah becomes someone Ishita can teach, which puts her back at the centre.

grounding: A boy's old friend acts cold after he makes a new friend; he feels guilty and cornered, then reassures her, keeps their time and invites her to include the newcomer.

passage:
The rain had cancelled the school bus, so Minakshi's father dropped her and Sachin, the new boy from her street, together. They laughed all the way about a cartoon dog. Minakshi loved it.
At the gate stood Rukhsar, her best friend. "Where were you? I waited at the bus stop in the rain."
Minakshi's stomach squeezed. "Oh, my dad was late," she said.
Then Sachin came up. "Thanks for the lift, Minakshi!"
Rukhsar's face closed like a door. Minakshi felt like a traitor twice over.
At break she found Rukhsar. "I lied. I came with Sachin. I like him, but you're still my best friend. I should have told you."

qa.q: Why was the school bus cancelled?
qa.a: The rain had cancelled it.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling after Sachin thanked her at the gate?
qa.a: She felt guilty, like a traitor twice over, because Rukhsar now knew she had lied about being late.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Minakshi lied about where she had been, which made Rukhsar more hurt; owning up and saying Rukhsar still mattered was the fix.

qa.q: What was it like for Rukhsar at the gate?
qa.a: Rukhsar had waited in the rain and then learned the excuse was untrue, so she felt hurt and shut out.

grounding: A girl enjoys a new friend but feels like a traitor to her old one; lying about where she was makes it worse, and honesty helps.

passage:
Harsha had found a new friend in Saurabh, who lived on the fourth floor of their Chennai building and knew every cricket rule. They'd played in the stilt parking all week.
But Pallavi, Harsha's friend since Class 1, had rung the bell twice, and both times Harsha's mother had said, "Harsha's downstairs." Harsha felt a heavy knot every time the bat swung, as if he were cheating on someone.
He thought about saying he was ill. Instead, on Saturday he knocked on Pallavi's door. "I've been playing cricket with Saurabh. It's fun. But you still matter to me. Come and bowl with us? Then board games at yours after?"
Pallavi grinned. "I bowl faster than you."

qa.q: Where did Harsha and Saurabh play cricket?
qa.a: In the stilt parking of their Chennai building.

qa.q: Why did Harsha feel a heavy knot while playing cricket?
qa.a: He felt guilty, as if he were cheating on Pallavi, because she had come looking for him twice while he was with Saurabh.

qa.q: Which choice did Harsha make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He told Pallavi the truth instead of pretending to be ill, and showed she still mattered by inviting her to bowl and planning board games together.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt after ringing the bell twice for nothing?
qa.a: Pallavi may have felt left out and puzzled, so hearing the truth and an invitation from Harsha would be a relief.

grounding: A boy likes his new friend but feels like a traitor to his old one; instead of lying, he tells her the truth and shows she still matters.

passage:
My name is Keerthana, and last year I joined Class 6 in the middle of term. Shreya was the first person to share her pencil box with me. But her old friend Bhoomi went silent every time I sat down near them. She'd turn her back and talk only to Shreya.
I felt like an intruder. Once I almost said, "Bhoomi always copies you, you know," just to make her look bad. I stopped myself. I knew Shreya would hate being pushed to pick.
So I kept saying good morning to Bhoomi, even when she didn't answer. I asked about her drawings. By the winter holidays, she was saving both of us a seat.

qa.q: Who was the first person to share a pencil box with Keerthana?
qa.a: Shreya was the first.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when Bhoomi turned her back?
qa.a: Keerthana felt like an intruder, unwanted and insecure, sensing that Bhoomi disliked the newcomer.

qa.q: Why was Keerthana's patient approach wiser than the remark she almost made?
qa.a: Making Bhoomi look bad would have pushed Shreya to choose, while staying friendly and giving it time let Bhoomi warm up.

qa.q: How might Bhoomi have seen Keerthana at first?
qa.a: Bhoomi may have felt threatened, as if the newcomer could take Shreya away, which explains her silence.

grounding: A newcomer senses that a new friend's old friend dislikes the newcomer, stays friendly, does not force a choice or run the other girl down, and gives it time.

passage:
Note from the class teacher, Class 4B, end of the month.
Suraj joined us three weeks ago and quickly became friends with Nazia. Nazia's old friend Tulsi has been cool towards him: she moves her bag onto the spare chair when he comes near. Suraj has noticed. On the first Monday he told a group that Tulsi "cries at everything", and the other children turned on him instead. He looked miserable.
Since then he has changed. He greets Tulsi every morning, never asks Nazia to choose, and lets the two girls walk ahead sometimes. Today Tulsi lent him her ruler. I plan to seat the three together for the craft fair.

qa.q: How did Suraj seem to feel after his remark about Tulsi backfired?

qa.q: What has Suraj done since then that is working?
qa.a: He greets Tulsi every morning, doesn't make Nazia choose, and gives the girls space, and Tulsi has started to warm up.

qa.q: What might Tulsi feel when Suraj keeps greeting her?
qa.a: Tulsi may slowly feel less threatened and see he isn't trying to take Nazia, which is why she lends him her ruler.

grounding: A newcomer senses his friend's old friend dislikes him; trying to make her look bad backfires, while staying friendly and giving time helps.

passage:
Note from the badminton coach, Saturday session.
Devika usually pairs with her best friend Swati. Today Swati arrived with a new girl, Ruth, and the two were chatting. Devika's face fell for a moment and she busied herself with her shoelaces.
Then she stood up, walked over and said, "Hi, Ruth. I'm Devika." A minute later she asked me if the three of them could play king of the court instead of doubles. They rotated for half an hour, laughing a lot. When I praised her, Devika shrugged and said, "It felt a bit weird at first, but it's more fun with three." I will pair Ruth with different girls next week too.

qa.q: What game did Devika suggest for the three girls?
qa.a: King of the court.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when she first saw Swati with Ruth?
qa.a: She felt a flash of hurt or disappointment; her face fell and she busied herself with her shoelaces.

qa.q: What did Devika do that showed generosity?
qa.a: She walked over, introduced herself to Ruth and suggested a game for three, instead of sulking or pulling Swati away.

qa.q: How might Ruth see Devika's hello?
qa.a: Ruth, being new, may feel relieved and welcomed rather than like an outsider between two old friends. 🙂

grounding: A girl sees her best friend with a new girl, feels a moment's hurt, then says hi and suggests a game for three, showing generosity rather than pretending.

passage:
Wednesday
Anjali brought the new girl, Tamsin, to our tree today. My first thought was, great, now I'm the extra one. I felt a little pinch in my chest.
But then I remembered Anjali has cousins and a dance class and she still always comes back to me. Friends are allowed other friends. It doesn't cost me much to be nice.
So I said, "Hi, Tamsin. Want to play three-way catch?" Tamsin can't catch at all, but she laughs at herself, which is funny. Anjali looked so happy.
I'm not going to pretend I didn't feel the pinch. But it went away faster than I thought.
Irfan

qa.q: What game did Irfan suggest to Tamsin?
qa.a: Three-way catch.

qa.q: What was Irfan's first feeling when Anjali brought Tamsin to the tree?
qa.a: A little pinch of jealousy, worried about becoming "the extra one".

qa.q: What helped Irfan choose to be friendly?
qa.a: Irfan remembered that Anjali has other friends and still comes back, so being kind to Tamsin cost little.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Irfan welcomes Tamsin?
qa.a: Anjali looked happy, likely relieved that her friends can get along without her having to choose. 😊

grounding: Irfan notices his best friend bringing a new girl, feels a small pang, then chooses to welcome her with a game for three, without pretending the pang wasn't there.

passage:
Tuesday night
Zeenat and the new girl did the science worksheet together again. They have a secret wave now. I sat and ate my lunch looking at my tiffin lid.
When I got home I didn't want to talk. Didi said, "Just ignore them," while scrolling, which made my throat feel tighter.
Then Mum came and sat on my bed while I was pretending to read. She said, "You've been quiet all week." I told her everything. She didn't tell me what to do. She said friendships shift and stretch, like a rubber band, and don't always snap. And she said, "I'm right here."
I don't feel fixed. But I feel less alone.
Shalini

qa.q: What do Zeenat and the new girl have now?
qa.a: They have a secret wave.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel after Didi said "Just ignore them"?
qa.a: Shalini felt more hurt and alone; Shalini's throat felt tighter, as if nobody was really listening.

qa.q: What did Mum do that helped more than advice?
qa.a: She noticed Shalini was quiet, listened to everything, explained that friendships shift and stretch, and said she was right there.

qa.q: How might Mum have seen Shalini's week?
qa.a: Mum had noticed the quietness all week and seems to understand that Shalini needed to be heard rather than told what to do.

grounding: Shalini, hurt by a friend's new friendship, is told to just ignore it, but Mum notices the quietness, listens, and reassures Shalini that friendships shift and she is there.

passage:
Payal and Maa were shelling peas in the courtyard when Maa put down the bowl. "You've barely spoken since Sunday."
Payal shrugged. Then, all at once: "Shreya goes to the tuition house with that new girl from the mill quarters. They walk together now. My brother said just forget her."
Maa listened without shelling a single pea. "When I was your age my best friend married and moved to the next village. I thought it was over. It wasn't. Friendships bend and grow. They make room. And I'm here, always."
Payal leaned against Maa's shoulder. She still felt sore, but her chest felt looser.

qa.q: What were Payal and Maa doing in the courtyard?
qa.a: They were shelling peas.

qa.q: How did Payal feel after talking with Maa?
qa.a: She still felt sore about Shreya, but lighter and comforted, with her chest feeling looser.

qa.q: What made Maa's response more helpful than the brother's?
qa.a: Maa stopped her work, listened fully and shared her own story, while "just forget her" left Payal alone with the hurt.

qa.q: How might Maa see Payal's silence since Sunday?
qa.a: Maa seems to read the silence as a sign something is hurting, which is why she stops and asks gently.

grounding: A girl upset that her friend walks with someone new is told to forget it by her brother, but her mother notices, listens and reassures her that friendships shift and she is there.

passage:
"Dolma, why were you sitting with Priyanka's group at lunch?"
"They asked me to help with their skit."
"You're MY partner. You always sit with me."
"Minakshi, it was just lunch."
"You didn't even look at me. Next time, say no to them."

qa.a: They asked her to help with their skit.

qa.q: What was Minakshi worried about underneath her anger?
qa.a: She was scared that Dolma wouldn't come back to her, which is why she tried to control where Dolma sat.

qa.q: What could Minakshi try next time she feels this way?
qa.a: She could tell Dolma she feels scared or left out, instead of giving orders, and trust that Dolma will come back.

qa.q: How did Minakshi's "caring" feel to Dolma?
qa.a: It felt suffocating to Dolma, as if she wasn't allowed to breathe or have other friends.

grounding: A girl treats her friend like property and gets angry when she sits with others; the friend explains it feels smothering, and the girl learns to trust her.

passage:
Looking back, I can see how I held Urmila too tight in Class 4. My name is Tushar, and she was my first real friend. When she joined the skipping girls at break, I pulled her sleeve and said she had to play marbles with me. When she lent her crayons to someone else, I sulked all afternoon. I told myself this was loyalty.
Then one day she just stopped talking to anyone, even the skipping girls, and sat alone. She looked smaller.
That scared me. I told her, "Go skip. I'll be at the marbles." She went. At the end of break she came running back to show me a new rhyme.

qa.q: What did Tushar want Urmila to play at break?
qa.a: Marbles.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when Urmila sat alone and looked smaller?
qa.a: Tushar felt scared, realising that holding her so tight had made her shrink.

qa.q: What changed things for the better?
qa.a: Tushar let Urmila go and skip with the other girls, trusting she would come back, and she came running back with a new rhyme.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt when Tushar pulled her sleeve and sulked?
qa.a: Urmila may have felt torn and trapped, as though having other friends would hurt Tushar.

grounding: A child looks back on treating a friend like property, sees how it shrank her, and learns that letting her go and trusting she will return is real friendship.

passage:
Monday. At break Avni asked, "Can I play with Rosie today?" Disha shrugged. "Fine. Go and play with Rosie." That night she drew a small tally mark on the back page of her rough book.
Thursday. Four tally marks now. When Avni waved, Disha didn't wave back. At the tap she almost told Rosie that Avni thought her plaits were silly. Her stomach turned; that wasn't even true.
Saturday. Disha called Avni. Her voice shook. "I said fine, but it wasn't fine. I felt left out, and I've been counting. I don't want to be mean."
Avni was quiet. "Thanks for telling me. Let's all three play Monday?"

qa.q: Where did Disha draw the tally marks?
qa.a: On the back page of her rough book.

qa.q: Why did Disha's stomach turn at the tap on Thursday?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, realising her silent resentment was pushing her to say something mean and untrue about Rosie.

qa.q: What did Disha do on Saturday that was wiser than keeping count?
qa.a: She told Avni calmly and honestly that she had felt left out, instead of letting the hurt grow into cruelty.

qa.q: How might Avni feel when she hears about the tally marks?
qa.a: Avni may feel surprised and a bit sad, but also grateful that Disha told her, since she suggests all three play together.

grounding: A girl says fine when her friend plays with someone else but keeps score; the resentment nearly turns cruel until she says the hurt out loud calmly.

passage:
"Sarita, sit with your Irfan Chacha a minute. When I was ten, my best friend was Nasreen, the girl next door. Then a new girl, Lalita, came to our school. Nasreen started playing hopscotch with her. I said, 'Fine, go and play with her,' like I didn't care.
But I cared. I counted every day she chose Lalita, like marks on a wall. After a month, I was so full of it that I hid Lalita's slate before a test. She cried. Nasreen looked at me as if she didn't know me.
If I'd just said once, calmly, 'I feel left out,' none of that would have happened."

qa.q: What did young Irfan hide before a test?
qa.a: He hid Lalita's slate.

qa.q: What was young Irfan really feeling when he said "Fine, go and play with her"?
qa.a: He felt hurt and left out but hid it, pretending not to care while counting every time Nasreen chose Lalita.

qa.q: What turning point in the story could Irfan have handled differently?
qa.a: At the start, he could have said calmly and once that he felt left out, instead of saying "fine" and silently keeping score.

qa.q: How did Nasreen see Irfan after the slate was hidden?
qa.a: Nasreen looked at him as if she didn't know him, shocked that her friend could be cruel.

grounding: An uncle recalls saying fine when his friend played with a new girl, silently keeping score until the resentment turned into cruelty, and wishing he had said the hurt calmly.
